evidence_spans.text: We select the same set of 871 subjects used by Abraham et al. (2017) that met the imaging quality and phenotypic information criteria, comprising 403 individuals with ASD and 468 healthy controls. These subjects were regrouped based on location into 20 imaging sites.
evidence_spans.claim: Cohort is the same 871-subject ABIDE I subset (403 ASD, 468 controls) as Abraham et al. 2017, from 20 sites.

evidence_spans.text: we use the same preprocessing pipeline, the Conﬁgurable Pipeline for the Analysis of Connectomes (C-PAC) (Craddock et al., 2013), which involves skull striping, slice timing correction, motion correction, global mean intensity normalisation, nuisance signal regression, band-pass ﬁltering (0.01- 0.1Hz)
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used C-PAC (skull stripping, motion correction, nuisance regression, band-pass filtering 0.01-0.1Hz).

evidence_spans.text: the mean time series for a set of regions extracted from the Harvard Oxford (HO) atlas (Desikan et al., 2006) were computed and normalised to zero mean and unit variance
evidence_spans.claim: Harvard-Oxford atlas used for ROI time-series extraction and connectivity feature construction.

evidence_spans.text: We evaluate our model on both the ADNI and ABIDE databases using a 10-fold stratiﬁed cross validation strategy.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation used 10-fold stratified cross-validation (not leave-site-out).

evidence_spans.text: We focus our attention to the phenotypic graph (using default phenotypic measures), which corresponds to the graph constructed taking into account SEX and SITE information, weighted by the feature correlation similarity.
evidence_spans.claim: The best-performing population graph uses sex and site as phenotypic edge-weighting measures alongside imaging feature similarity.

evidence_spans.text: In Parisot et al. (2017), we used a ridge classiﬁer to perform Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) with a ﬁxed number of features C. It is an iterative process, where each iteration trains the ridge classiﬁer on the training set with the current feature vector.
evidence_spans.claim: Feature selection (RFE) was trained on the training set within the cross-validation scheme.

evidence_spans.text: The best average performance is achieved for K = 4 with accuracy 70.4% and AUC 0.75.
evidence_spans.claim: Best GCN classification result on ABIDE: 70.4% accuracy, AUC 0.75, with a K=4 Chebyshev polynomial order on the phenotypic graph.

evidence_spans.text: Our experiments suggest that an accuracy of approx. 70% could be an intrinsic limitation of the whole dataset.
evidence_spans.claim: Authors interpret the ~70% accuracy ceiling as a possible intrinsic limitation of the heterogeneous multi-site ABIDE dataset.

assessments.support: Reuses the well-documented 871-subject (403 ASD/468 control), 20-site ABIDE I subset from Abraham et al. 2017.
Harvard-Oxford atlas, C-PAC pipeline, and multiple feature-selection strategies (RFE, PCA, MLP, autoencoder) explicitly described and compared.
Diagnostic label (ASD vs control) inherited from ABIDE phenotypic file; no specific diagnostic instrument/criteria stated in this paper.

Evaluation uses 10-fold stratified CV (not site-held-out) despite site being a known confound, and the GCN is semi-supervised/transductive: unlabelled test-node imaging features and phenotypic edges are present in the graph during training, even though RFE itself is fit on training folds only.

risk_of_bias.summary: Methodologically transparent predictive GCN study on a well-characterised ABIDE subset, but site-stratified (not site-held-out) CV and transductive graph construction leave open whether reported accuracy generalises to unseen sites.

assessments.support: Explicit site-level inclusion rules (raw uncorrected scans, >=8 min scan duration, >=15 ASD individuals), yielding 7 of 16 ABIDE sites and 605 participants (304 ASD, 301 CT).
